title: Food & drink
goal: Name everyday Odia foods, say you're hungry or thirsty, say what you like, and order in a restaurant.
intro: Odia food revolves around **ଭାତ** (rice), **ଡାଲି** (dal) and **ତରକାରୀ** (vegetable curries), plus fish and the famous summer dish **ପଖାଳ** — rice soaked in water. Grammatically, this unit introduces the **dative subject**: in Odia, hunger 'strikes *to* you' (ମୋତେ ଭୋକ ଲାଗୁଛି), and liking something means it 'feels good *to* you'.

vocab.note: People often say ଚା ଖାଇବା 'eat tea' as well as ଚା ପିଇବା.
Odisha's iconic summer food, eaten with fried/roasted sides.
ତରକାରୀ ବହୁତ ରାଗ 'the curry is very spicy'.
Lunch: ଦିନ ଖାଇବା; dinner: ରାତି ଖାଇବା.
ମୁଁ ପଖାଳ ଭଲ ପାଏ 'I love pakhala'.

vocab.en: to feel, seem; to be applied
vocab.note: With dative: ମୋତେ ଭଲ ଲାଗେ 'I like it'.

grammar.title: Dative subjects: ମୋତେ ଭୋକ ଲାଗୁଛି
grammar.body:
Feelings, needs and likes are often expressed with the person in the **dative** (to-me) form and the thing as the grammatical subject:
ମୋତେ ଭୋକ ଲାଗୁଛି — *to-me hunger is-striking* — 'I'm hungry'
ମୋତେ ମାଛ ଭଲ ଲାଗେ — *to-me fish good feels* — 'I like fish'
ମୋତେ ପାଣି ଦରକାର — *to-me water needed* — 'I need water'

Dative pronouns: **ମୋତେ** me · **ଆମକୁ** us · **ତୋତେ** you (intimate) · **ତୁମକୁ** you (familiar) · **ଆପଣଙ୍କୁ** you (formal) · **ତାକୁ** him/her · **ତାଙ୍କୁ** him/her (resp.) · **ସେମାନଙ୍କୁ** them. With nouns add **-କୁ** (*-ku*): ପିଲାକୁ 'to the child'.

The verb ଲାଗିବା stays the same whoever the person is: ଲାଗେ (generally), ଲାଗୁଛି (right now), ଲାଗିଲା (felt).

examples.native: ତାଙ୍କୁ ରାଗ ଖାଇବା ଭଲ ଲାଗେ ନାହିଁ।
examples.roman: taṅku ragô khaiba bhôlô lage nahiṃ.

grammar.title: Want, love, and ordering
grammar.body:
With an ordinary subject you can also say:
**ମୁଁ … ଭଲ ପାଏ** — I love/really like … (ଆପଣ ଭଲ ପାଆନ୍ତି, ତୁମେ ଭଲ ପାଅ)
**ମୁଁ … ଚାହେଁ** — I want … (polite, slightly formal)

To **order**, use a polite command: **ଦିଅନ୍ତୁ** 'please give', **ଆଣନ୍ତୁ** 'please bring'. To make it negative, add ନାହିଁ: ଦିଅନ୍ତୁ ନାହିଁ 'please don't give'.

The **future** tense is the polite way to offer: ଆପଣ କ'ଣ ଖାଇବେ? 'What will you eat?', ଚା ପିଇବେ? 'Will you have tea?'. Present negative: ମୁଁ ମାଂସ ଖାଏ ନାହିଁ (colloquially ଖାଏନି).

examples.en: I'd like a cup of tea.
Bring two plates of rice, please.

dialogue.title: Lunch at a roadside 'hotel'
dialogue.setting: Sam stops for lunch at a small eatery near Puri on a hot day.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: Come in, sit down. What will you have?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: ଭାତ, ଡାଲି, ଦାଲମା, ମାଛ ତରକାରୀ, ଆଉ ପଖାଳ ବି ଅଛି।
lines.roman: bhatô, ḍali, dalma, machhô tôrôkari, au pôkhaḷô bi achhi.
lines.en: Rice, dal, dalma, fish curry — and there's pakhala too.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: ପାଣିରେ ଭିଜା ଭାତ। ଖରାଦିନେ ବହୁତ ଭଲ ଲାଗେ।
lines.roman: paṇire bhija bhatô. khôradine bôhutô bhôlô lage.
lines.en: Rice soaked in water. It's lovely in the hot season.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ଠିକ୍ ଅଛି, ଗୋଟିଏ ପଖାଳ ଥାଳି ଦିଅନ୍ତୁ। କିନ୍ତୁ ବେଶି ରାଗ ନୁହେଁ।
lines.roman: ṭhik achhi, goṭie pôkhaḷô thaḷi diôntu. kintu besi ragô nuheṃ.
lines.en: Okay, one pakhala thali please. But not too spicy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Yes, a lassi and some water.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: A hundred and twenty rupees, sir.

culture: Small restaurants in Odisha are often called **ହୋଟେଲ** ('hotel') even if they have no rooms. A meal is traditionally eaten with the right hand. On 20 March Odias celebrate *Pakhala Dibasa* (Pakhala Day). Jagannath temple's **ମହାପ୍ରସାଦ** (cooked offering of rice, dal and vegetables) is sold at Puri's Ananda Bazar and shared by all castes — a symbol of equality. Famous sweets include ରସଗୋଲା, ଛେନାପୋଡ଼ (baked cheese) and ଖିରି.
